cases.name: c1.constant_velocity_worldline
cases.notes: the constant-velocity model is a VERIFICATION MODEL ONLY: it needs infinite acceleration at both ends. It earns its place because tau = t/gamma is exact, which makes it the right instrument for testing the proper-time integrator
cases.reference: x = v t for a constant coordinate velocity of 0.5 c over 4 yr

cases.name: c1.proper_time_integration
cases.notes: constant integrand, so Simpson is exact here up to rounding; the accelerated case below is the one that exercises the quadrature order
cases.reference: Simpson integration of dtau = dt sqrt(1-beta^2) against the exact tau = t/gamma at beta = 0.8

cases.name: c1.proper_acceleration_analytic_position
cases.notes: 1 g is 0.31648 pc/yr^2, converted in one place from the defined 9.80665 m/s^2; a/c is 1.0322952755535963 per year, the familiar 'one gravity is about one c per year'
cases.reference: x(tau) = (c^2/a)[cosh(a tau/c) - 1] at 1 g for tau = 2 yr

cases.name: c1.proper_acceleration_analytic_coordinate_time
cases.notes: coordinate time already exceeds proper time by 1.8781447248904473 at only two years of ship time
cases.reference: c t(tau) = (c^2/a) sinh(a tau/c) at 1 g for tau = 2 yr

cases.name: c1.proper_acceleration_analytic_velocity_and_gamma
cases.notes: the three relations are checked together because a wrong rapidity can satisfy any one of them alone
cases.reference: beta = tanh(a tau/c), gamma = cosh(a tau/c), and gamma = 1/sqrt(1-beta^2) all agree

cases.name: c1.symmetric_journey_endpoint
cases.notes: total ship time 3.5420808280945368 yr against coordinate time 5.8725514839370438 yr, peak beta 0.94965327739394345
cases.reference: a symmetric 1 g journey arrives at the destination distance and at rest

cases.computed_description: Proxima residual 7.4851236320228054e-13 pc in 39 iterations; Barnard residual 8.3000273320976703e-13 pc in 38 iterations
cases.name: c1.moving_destination_interception
cases.notes: bisection, not Newton: the residual is monotone in t for any profile bounded by c, so bracketing cannot diverge
cases.reference: the interception solve converges and places the ship on the destination's worldline, not at its catalogue position

cases.expected_description: Barnard's error exceeds Proxima's, and both are nonzero
cases.name: c1.stale_position_targeting_error
cases.notes: the comparison is the assertion: Barnard's star has the largest proper motion of any known star, so if the stale error were not larger for it the propagator would be wrong
cases.reference: aiming at the stale catalogue position misses, and misses more for the faster-moving star

cases.expected_description: arrival sigma at least the epoch sigma
cases.name: c1.interception_uncertainty
cases.notes: this is the number that decides whether you arrive in the system or merely near it, and it is not the catalogue's quoted error
cases.reference: the interception position uncertainty exceeds the catalogue position uncertainty, because velocity errors integrate over the flight

cases.name: c1.lorentz_norm_preservation
cases.notes: the boost is written out in full rather than as a rotation to the z axis plus a 1-D boost, because the round trip through a rotation is where an axis convention slips in unnoticed. The tolerance is a few ulps on order-one quantities, not a physical allowance: the norm is preserved EXACTLY in real arithmetic and the residual here is the rounding of the gamma products
cases.reference: the boost preserves the Minkowski norm of a null and a timelike four-vector, and the four-velocity is unit timelike

cases.name: c1.aberration_analytic
cases.notes: implemented by boosting the photon four-vector; the scalar formula is the TEST, not the implementation, which is the right way round because the boost generalises to any velocity direction
cases.reference: the four-vector boost reproduces cos t' = (cos t + b)/(1 + b cos t) for the source direction, over 37 angles

cases.expected_description: cos of the apparent angle never below the geometric one
cases.name: c1.aberration_crowds_toward_motion
cases.notes: the case that catches a sign inversion. Reproducing one formula from itself would pass with the sign wrong; this asserts the physical direction of the effect
cases.reference: apparent source positions crowd toward the direction of motion at every angle

cases.name: c1.doppler_approaching
cases.notes: computed from -(u_ship.k)/(u_ref.k), so the longitudinal limit is a consequence rather than the definition. D = 2 is a blueshift, as it must be for an approaching source
cases.reference: nu'/nu = sqrt((1+b)/(1-b)) for a source directly ahead

cases.name: c1.doppler_receding
cases.notes: the reciprocal of the approaching case to 0. The transverse case gives 1.25 = gamma, pure time dilation, which has no classical counterpart
cases.reference: nu'/nu = sqrt((1-b)/(1+b)) for a source directly behind

cases.name: c1.zero_velocity_sky_recovery_doppler
cases.notes: tolerance ZERO and it holds: boost() returns its argument unchanged when beta is zero, and the time component was set to the frequency exactly
cases.reference: at zero velocity every Doppler factor is exactly 1

cases.name: c1.zero_velocity_sky_recovery_directions
cases.notes: the tolerance is four ulps and the reason is stated rather than assumed: the input direction (cos t, sin t, 0) has norm 1 only to rounding, and the code renormalises it. A stationary observer's sky is the geometric sky to the last bit the representation allows
cases.reference: at zero velocity every apparent direction equals the geometric direction to within one renormalisation rounding

cases.name: c1.retarded_source_state
cases.notes: the star is seen where it WAS 4.2460387980143866 yr earlier, at epoch 2021.7539612019857, not where it is
cases.reference: the emission time satisfies |x_obs - x_star(t_e)| = c (t_obs - t_e)

cases.name: c1.earth_to_ship_signal_delay
cases.notes: this is NOT 'the current time on Earth'. It is the latest Earth event whose light has arrived, 1.4154866411349765 yr stale, and no display aboard the ship may show otherwise
cases.parameters: one third of the way to Proxima
cases.reference: the Earth clock the ship can SEE lags coordinate time by |x|/c

cases.name: c1.ship_to_earth_signal_delay
cases.notes: round trip 2.8309732822699529 yr; the destination signal solve is separate because the destination MOVES and the outgoing light cone has to catch it
cases.parameters: one third of the way to Proxima
cases.reference: a message sent by the ship reaches Earth at t + |x|/c, and the round trip is 2|x|/c

cases.name: c1.apparent_sky_source_count
cases.notes: aberration MOVES stars, it never creates or destroys them; a row count that changed with beta would mean the renderer and the science disagree about what is in the sky
cases.reference: the apparent-sky table has exactly one row per placeable catalogue source, in both the rest and moving observer frames

cases.name: c1.uncertainty_angle_propagation
cases.notes: sigma/d is a small-angle statement; at 0.034074858474507121 rad the neglected term is of order its cube, which is beyond the fourth decimal
cases.reference: every apparent-sky row carries a finite, non-negative angular uncertainty, and the small-angle form remains defensible

cases.name: c1.deterministic_worldline
cases.notes: tolerance ZERO. Every visual downstream is generated from these samples, so a worldline that is merely reproducible to a tolerance would make animation frames irreproducible
cases.reference: rebuilding the worldline from the same inputs reproduces it bit for bit

title: C1-RELATIVISTIC-ASTROGATION: ship worldlines, clocks, moving-target interception, aberration, Doppler and the retarded apparent sky
